T1: Home barista demand is driven by social interaction and the desire to replicate the café experience at home, making premium equipment a social status purchase rather than a functional necessity. Who benefits: Simonelli Group can capture higher margins by positioning machines as status symbols for home baristas who seek to host or share coffee experiences.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers substitute the café for home use because the café offers a third place for social interaction, which they cannot replicate at home. This shifts purchase motivation from pure coffee quality to the social experience.. How value is captured: Simonelli can charge premium prices for machines with design, branding, and storytelling that emphasize the social aspect, and sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels that highlight the experience.. Assumptions: Home barista market is large enough to support premium pricing.; Consumers are willing to pay more for machines that signal social status and a curated coffee experience.; Simonelli can effectively communicate the social aspect of its machines to consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced home barista machine with social branding, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard professional machine.; Surveyed home baristas will rank social experience as a top factor in purchase decisions.; Willingness to pay for the social aspect will exceed willingness to pay for functional improvements alone..

T2: Home barista demand is driven by convenience and the desire for consistent, high-quality coffee at home, making machines a functional necessity rather than a status purchase. Who benefits: Simonelli Group can capture value by offering reliable, easy-to-use machines that meet daily coffee needs, generating repeat purchases and loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers adopt home barista equipment to save time and ensure consistent coffee quality, viewing it as a practical solution for busy lifestyles rather than a social status item.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price machines competitively, emphasize convenience features (e.g., automatic grinding, single-serve), and sell through retail channels that highlight ease of use.. Assumptions: Convenience and consistency are primary purchase drivers for home baristas.; Consumers are willing to pay for machines that reduce preparation time and ensure quality.; Simonelli can differentiate its machines through convenience features without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a convenience-focused home barista machine, purchase intent will be higher than for a premium-priced social branding machine.; Surveyed home baristas will rank convenience as a top factor in purchase decisions.; Willingness to pay for convenience features will exceed willingness to pay for design or social branding..
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

T1: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a visible status signal, because conspicuous consumption increases purchase when income is linked to social status. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher margins and brand prestige by selling premium home machines as status items.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers with higher income and status values are more likely to publicly display purchases of visible goods, leading to increased demand when the purchase is framed as a status statement.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price premium home machines and capture higher margins by positioning them as status items rather than purely functional tools.. Assumptions: Status-driven consumers are a significant segment of the home coffee market.; Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to these consumers.; The current professional brand does not cannibalize the consumer proposition.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed as a status item, purchase intent among high-income consumers increases relative to a functional positioning.; Sales of the status-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed purely as a functional product..

T2: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a functional, reliable tool for consistent coffee quality, because reliability reduces purchase hesitation and increases repeat purchases. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains repeat sales and customer loyalty by providing a product that delivers consistent results, increasing overall revenue.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers purchase coffee equipment when they trust the product will perform reliably, reducing the perceived risk of buying a new machine.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price its home machines as reliable, high-quality tools and capture value through repeat purchases and service contracts.. Assumptions: Reliability is a primary purchase driver for home coffee equipment.; Simonelli’s existing professional reputation transfers to consumer positioning.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product they trust to perform consistently.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed on reliability and consistent performance, purchase intent among consumers increases relative to a machine marketed on status.; Sales of the reliability-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed on status..

Test "Status vs Reliability Choice Experiment" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase of a home espresso machine. Participants view two machine descriptions: one emphasizing status visibility and social prestige, the other emphasizing reliability and consistent performance. They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase each machine and to state their maximum price they would pay. The experiment is randomly assigned to either the status or reliability framing.. Sample: 300 adult consumers interested in home coffee equipment, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and self-reported coffee consumption frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay for each framing.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the status-framed machine compared to the reliability-framed machine.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the reliability-framed machine compared to the status-framed machine.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay for the status-framed machine exceeds the average willingness to pay for the reliability-framed machine by at least 10%, we conclude that status framing drives purchase decisions and recommend developing a status-positioned consumer proposition. If the difference is below 10%, we conclude that reliability framing drives purchase decisions and recommend a reliability-positioned proposition. If the difference is not statistically significant, we recommend further research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Simonelli already offers a home-focused machine (Linea Micra) and has a consumer line (Oscar Mood), but it does not demonstrate that status-driven demand will generate sufficient sales to justify the investment. A limited test is needed to measure whether status framing drives purchase decisions. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Simonelli already offers a home-focused machine (Linea Micra) and has a consumer line (Oscar Mood), but it does not demonstrate that status-driven demand will generate sufficient sales to justify the investment. A limited test is needed to measure whether status framing drives purchase decisions. Target customer: Home coffee consumers who value visible status and social prestige, particularly high-income individuals who purchase coffee equipment as a conspicuous status item.. Value proposition: A premium home espresso machine positioned as a status item that signals social prestige and elevates the home coffee experience, leveraging Simonelli’s existing professional reputation and design.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 12‑week, €20,000 online choice experiment comparing status versus reliability framing to determine whether status drives purchase decisions. If the status framing yields a statistically significant willingness-to-pay edge,. Uncertainty: The size of the status-driven consumer segment and Simonelli’s ability to capture higher margins from a status proposition remain uncertain. The evidence also does not address whether reliability, visibility, or other factors influence. Would change if: If the test shows the reliability framing yields a statistically significant willingness-to-pay edge, we would shift to a reliability‑positioned consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference between framing, we would recommend further research on consumer purchase drivers.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.. Assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.; A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.; Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.; Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution that reduces the hassle of bottled water or other alternative water sources. Who benefits: Busy households and consumers who currently spend time and money on bottled water, delivery services, or other water alternatives.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin offers a membrane that is easy to install, requires minimal maintenance (e.g., cartridge replacement indicator), and integrates with smart home systems, consumers will switch from the hassle of bottled water to a single, self‑s. How value is captured: Lower upfront cost compared to premium membrane, subscription services for maintenance, and data‑driven insights that enhance convenience through smart home integration.. Assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.; A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.; Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher repeat purchase rates than standard membranes.; Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members..

Does not show: It does not show that a premium positioning would change this preference, nor does it quantify willingness to pay for a differentiated membrane..

T2 supports, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "The user friendliness continues, as ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.". Does not show: It does not demonstrate that consumers currently find bottled water inconvenient or that a low‑maintenance membrane would be attractive, nor does it quantify willingness to pay for convenience..

Test "Messaging Test: Premium vs Convenience Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with between‑subjects design. Participants view two versions of a product description (premium vs convenience) for the same membrane. They select which version they would purchase and indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and perceived importance of attributes (taste, safety, convenience, maintenance).. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a representative Danish population.. Measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary: would purchase premium vs convenience version). Secondary outcomes: WTP (max price participants would pay) and importance ratings (1‑10).. Predictions: T1: Premium messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher WTP than convenience messaging, because health‑enhancing positioning aligns with T1’s claim that premium perception drives adoption.; T2: Convenience messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher WTP than premium messaging, because low‑maintenance positioning aligns with T2’s claim that convenience reduces perceived effort and drives adoption.. Decision rule: If premium messaging achieves at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than convenience messaging, and the difference in WTP is at least €10, then T1 is supported and a differentiated premium consumer proposition is justified.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience, particularly in Denmark and potentially other markets where tap water quality is perceived as uncertain.. Value proposition: A high‑performance membrane that eliminates taste concerns, provides clear health benefits, and offers easy installation and low maintenance, enabling premium pricing and subscription services for maintenance.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed messaging test (500 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare premium vs. convenience messaging and determine whether premium positioning drives higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium‑willing segment, actual willingness to pay, and the ability to scale production and distribution remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand for a differentiated proposition is needed before committing resources.. Would change if: If the messaging test shows convenience messaging achieving at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent and a €10 price premium, or if a survey reveals that taste/safety is the primary barrier to tap water use, we would shift focus; to a convenience‑focused proposition and explore low‑upfront‑cost models.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

Test "Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (focus on health benefits, taste, and purity) or Sustainability Condition (focus on reducing plastic waste and environmental impact). Both conditions present a differentiated home water purifier at the same price point. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income levels.. Measure: Purchase intent score in the Premium Condition versus the Sustainability Condition, and maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If Premium Condition purchase intent exceeds Sustainability Condition by at least 10 points (e.g., Premium ≥ 65, Sustainability ≤ 55) AND the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If Sustainability Condition exceeds Premium Condition by at least 10 points AND the difference is statistically significant, proceed with a sustainability‑focused proposition. If neither condition meets the threshold, do not expand the consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium for taste and purity, nor does it show demand for a differentiated product. The company’s financial performance and strategic review indicate ongoing challenges, and any expansion must be justified by observable demand. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer willingness to pay a premium for taste and purity, nor does it provide evidence of consumer demand for a differentiated product. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium for taste and purity, nor does it show demand for a differentiated product. The company’s financial performance and strategic review indicate ongoing challenges, and any expansion must be justified by observable demand. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Value proposition: A differentiated home water purifier positioned as a premium, easy‑to‑use solution that delivers superior taste and purity, sold through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct the proposed Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for taste and purity before any investment.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company claims and independent studies that do not directly measure consumer demand, price sensitivity, or willingness to pay for a differentiated product.. Would change if: If the test shows the Premium Condition purchase intent exceeds the Sustainability Condition by at least 10 points and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we would proceed with a differentiated premium consumer strategy.; If the test shows the Sustainability Condition purchase intent exceeds the Premium Condition by at least 10 points and the difference is statistically significant, we would pursue a sustainability‑focused proposition.; If neither condition meets the threshold, we would maintain the current B2B focus and not expand the consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt professional-grade laundry equipment if they perceive it as a premium, long‑life product that reduces their own laundry effort and costs. Who benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently do laundry themselves and seek convenience and cost savings.. Why behaviour changes: They will switch from doing laundry at home to using a professional machine because they view it as a professional-grade, long‑term investment that saves time and money compared to domestic appliances.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by pricing the consumer offering at a premium (e.g., 20‑30% above domestic models) and selling through retail channels, leveraging its professional reputation to command higher prices.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for professional‑grade reliability and durability.; The perception of professional quality influences purchase decisions.; Retail distribution is feasible without disrupting the professional business.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑grade machine at a 25% premium over a comparable domestic model, at least 15% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales conversion rate will be higher in a retail setting than online, indicating demand for physical interaction..

T2: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt professional-grade laundry equipment if they need a reliable, high‑capacity solution for multi‑family buildings, student housing, or commercial spaces where domestic appliances are insufficient. Who benefits: Multi‑family property owners, property managers, and small business owners who require a durable, high‑volume washing and drying unit.. Why behaviour changes: They will switch from domestic appliances to professional machines because they need a unit that can handle multiple loads daily, reduces downtime, and provides consistent performance for a large number of users.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering high‑capacity models with extended warranties and service contracts, and by selling through wholesale channels to property managers and rental companies.. Assumptions: High‑volume demand exists in multi‑family and commercial settings.; Consumers are willing to invest in a professional machine for operational reliability.; Wholesale distribution can reach these segments effectively.. Test "Consumer vs Multi‑Family Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from homeowners and small business owners. Half see a consumer‑grade machine described as a premium, long‑life home appliance (T1). The other half see a high‑capacity machine described as a reliable, high‑volume solution for multi‑family buildings (T2). Both see identical product specifications and pricing (e.g., 25% premium over domestic models). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale and whether they would purchase now or in 12 weeks.. Sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel targeting homeowners and small business owners in the U.S.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and binary purchase intent (yes/no).. Predictions: T1: Consumer group will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion than multi‑family group.; T2: Multi‑family group will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion than consumer group.. Decision rule: If the consumer group’s average purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher than the multi‑family group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a consumer proposition and focus on the professional business.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial‑quality home appliances and that Electron‑x already sells consumer‑operated units, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners will pay a premium or that they need high‑capacity units. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Multi‑Family Messaging Test to measure purchase intent before committing. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not address T1, as it tests the effect of durability and repairability messaging on purchase reservations, not consumer willingness to pay a premium for professional-grade reliability. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial‑quality home appliances and that Electron‑x already sells consumer‑operated units, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners will pay a premium or that they need high‑capacity units. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Multi‑Family Messaging Test to measure purchase intent before committing. Target customer: Homeowners and small business owners who currently do laundry themselves and seek convenience and cost savings.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions professional‑grade laundry equipment as a premium, long‑life home appliance, leveraging Electron‑x’s professional reputation to command higher prices through retail channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer vs Multi‑Family Messaging Test (400 participants, 10 weeks, €18,000) to compare purchase intent for a premium‑grade consumer machine versus a high‑capacity multi‑family machine.. Uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for professional‑grade reliability and the size of the addressable market remain uncertain. The test will resolve whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.. Would change if: If the test shows the consumer group’s purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher than the multi‑family group, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners.; If the test shows no significant difference or lower intent, we would reconsider expansion and focus on the professional business.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt self‑service laundry solutions if they perceive lower operational costs and higher uptime, leading them to purchase dedicated machines for multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other shared spaces. Who benefits: Residents, guests, and members in multi‑family buildings and shared facilities benefit from reduced labor costs and increased machine uptime.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from hiring laundry services to self‑service machines when they calculate that the upfront cost is offset by long‑term savings and reduced downtime.. How value is captured: Electrolux captures value by selling premium‑priced machines and offering service contracts that ensure uptime and performance.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for machines that reduce long‑term operational costs.; Uptime and reliability are critical decision factors for consumers.; Electrolux can deliver on the performance claims and provide service support.. Predictions: In a survey, consumers will indicate that they would choose a self‑service machine if it promises at least a 10% reduction in monthly laundry costs compared to a traditional laundromat.; Willingness to pay for a self‑service machine will be higher when paired with a warranty covering downtime.; Adoption rates will be higher in multi‑family buildings and student housing than in single‑family homes..

T2: Consumers will adopt self‑service laundry solutions if they perceive the convenience of running their own laundry, reducing the need to wait for a laundromat or hire a service, leading them to purchase machines for multi‑family buildings and shared spaces. Who benefits: Residents, guests, and members in multi‑family buildings and shared facilities benefit from the convenience of self‑service laundry.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from relying on external laundry services to self‑service machines when convenience becomes a primary decision factor, especially in spaces where time and effort are limited.. How value is captured: Electrolux captures value by selling machines that are easy to operate and integrate with existing building infrastructure, and by offering support services that ensure smooth operation.. Assumptions: Consumers value time savings and convenience over cost savings.; Self‑service machines are perceived as user‑friendly and easy to operate.; Electrolux can provide clear instructions and support for consumers.. Predictions: In a survey, consumers will rank convenience as the top reason for choosing a self‑service machine, above cost or uptime.; Adoption rates will be higher in multi‑family buildings and student housing than in single‑family homes.; Consumers will be willing to pay a premium for machines that offer a simple, one‑button operation..

Test "Segmented Messaging Test for Consumer Laundry Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from residential (homeowners/renters) and small business (gyms, marinas, student housing) segments. Each participant sees one of three product descriptions: (1) compact consumer‑grade machine emphasizing convenience and cost savings; (2) compact consumer‑grade machine emphasizing remote management and small‑space suitability; (3) standard professional‑grade machine (control). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 residential (homeowners/renters) and 150 small businesses (gyms, marinas, student housing). Stratified random sampling within each segment.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for the described product.. Predictions: T1: Residential segment will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the convenience/cost‑saving message than the small‑business segment.; T2: Small‑business segment will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the remote management/compact‑space message than the residential segment.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience/cost‑saving message in the residential segment exceeds the average purchase intent for the remote management/compact‑space message in the small‑business segment by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 6.5 vs 5.0), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If the small‑business segment’s intent exceeds the residential segment’s intent by at least 1.5 points, develop a proposition targeting small businesses. If neither segment’s intent exceeds the other by at least 1.5 points, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the water source as unsafe or unhealthy, leading them to choose a branded home water filter that promises safety and taste. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or are concerned about tap water quality.. Why behaviour changes: Negative perceptions of tap water (e.g., taste, safety concerns) create a willingness to pay for a branded, controlled water source that promises purity and taste.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can charge a premium for a branded consumer product, sell directly to consumers, and capture margin through brand differentiation and repeat cartridge sales.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of tap water quality issues and actively seek alternatives.; Brand perception of safety and taste is a primary driver of purchase decisions.; Consumers are willing to pay more for a branded, controlled water source than for unbranded options.. Predictions: In markets where tap water quality is perceived as low, consumer surveys will show higher intent to purchase a branded home water filter.; Sales of a differentiated consumer product will be positively correlated with awareness of tap water safety concerns.; Willingness to pay for a branded product will exceed that for unbranded alternatives in the same segment..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the water source as a premium, healthful product, leading them to choose a branded home water filter for lifestyle and status reasons. Who benefits: Affluent, health-conscious consumers who view water as a premium commodity and seek a branded, high-end water experience.. Why behaviour changes: Perceived premium status and health benefits create a willingness to pay for a branded, high-end water source that differentiates from generic tap water.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can charge premium prices for a branded consumer product, sell through premium channels, and capture value through brand equity and repeat purchases.. Assumptions: Consumers associate brand prestige with water quality and health.; Premium pricing is acceptable for a differentiated water product.; Lifestyle and status are significant purchase drivers for this segment.. Predictions: In markets where water is perceived as a luxury good, consumer surveys will show higher intent to purchase a branded premium water product.; Sales of a differentiated consumer product will be positively correlated with brand perception of luxury and health.; Premium pricing will be accepted by a significant portion of the target segment..

Method: Run a targeted online survey with a sample of 500 adults in a region where tap water quality is perceived as low or moderate (e.g., a country with historical water safety concerns). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Safety message emphasizing tap water safety and health benefits; (B) Premium message emphasizing brand prestige, healthful water, and lifestyle appeal. Both messages. Sample: 500 adults (250 per condition) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of the target region.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (EUR) for a branded home water filter. Secondary measure: stated reason for purchase.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition B, indicating safety-driven demand.; T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition A, indicating premium positioning drives demand.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed to develop a safety-driven differentiated consumer proposition. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 1.5. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

T1: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, convenience solution that reduces their own laundry time and effort. Who benefits: Homeowners with limited time or space who currently do laundry themselves or use public laundromats.. Why behaviour changes: They would switch from manual laundry or public laundromats to a consumer‑operated setup because it saves time and effort, offering a convenience they value.. How value is captured: Electrolux would capture value through premium pricing, subscription services for maintenance, and potential licensing of the consumer‑operated model to other brands.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for convenience and reliability.; The consumer‑operated model can be scaled without compromising performance.; Regulatory and safety standards for consumer‑operated setups are achievable.. Predictions: In a survey, homeowners would indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for a consumer‑operated laundry solution compared to a standard professional machine.; Pilot deployment in a small residential building would show at least 20% uptake within 12 weeks.; Customers would report reduced laundry time and increased satisfaction compared to traditional methods..

T2: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a sustainable, eco‑friendly solution that aligns with their environmental values and reduces waste. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious homeowners who value sustainability and are willing to pay for eco‑friendly products.. Why behaviour changes: They would switch from traditional laundry methods to a consumer‑operated setup because it offers a sustainable alternative that reduces water and energy consumption, aligning with their values.. How value is captured: Electrolux would capture value through premium pricing for eco‑friendly features, subscription services for maintenance and recycling programs, and potential partnerships with sustainability‑focused brands.. Assumptions: Environmental awareness among homeowners is high enough to drive purchase decisions.; The consumer‑operated model can be equipped with eco‑friendly features without compromising performance.; Regulatory incentives or consumer demand for sustainable appliances exist in the target market.. Predictions: In a survey, homeowners would indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for an eco‑friendly consumer‑operated laundry solution compared to a standard professional machine.; Pilot deployment in a small residential building would show at least 25% uptake within 12 weeks among environmentally conscious households.; Customers would report higher satisfaction with reduced environmental impact compared to traditional methods..

Sample: 200 homeowners (100 per group) recruited via online panels, stratified by environmental awareness and time constraints.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros for each concept, and self‑reported intent to purchase or rent the solution within 12 months.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the convenience‑focused concept exceeds the eco‑focused concept by at least 10% points, recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

T1: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a visible status signal, because conspicuous consumption increases purchase when income is linked to social status. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher margins and brand prestige by selling premium home machines as status items.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers with higher income and status values are more likely to publicly display purchases of visible goods, leading to increased demand when the purchase is framed as a status statement.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price premium home machines and capture higher margins by positioning them as status items rather than purely functional tools.. Assumptions: Status-driven consumers are a significant segment of the home coffee market.; Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to these consumers.; The current professional brand does not cannibalize the consumer proposition.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed as a status item, purchase intent among high-income consumers increases relative to a functional positioning.; Sales of the status-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed purely as a functional product..

T2: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a functional, reliable tool for consistent coffee quality, because reliability reduces purchase hesitation and increases repeat purchases. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains repeat sales and customer loyalty by providing a product that delivers consistent results, increasing overall revenue.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers purchase coffee equipment when they trust the product will perform reliably, reducing the perceived risk of buying a new machine.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price its home machines as reliable, high-quality tools and capture value through repeat purchases and service contracts.. Assumptions: Reliability is a primary purchase driver for home coffee equipment.; Simonelli’s existing professional reputation transfers to consumer positioning.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product they trust to perform consistently.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed on reliability and consistent performance, purchase intent among consumers increases relative to a machine marketed on status.; Sales of the reliability-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed on status..

Test "Status vs Reliability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) status positioning (e.g., 'Oscar Mood is the Italian manufacturer’s first step towards a new frontier and a status item for home coffee enthusiasts.') or (B) reliability positioning (e.g., 'Oscar Mood is equipped with PID technology and ensures professional-quality coffee at home, delivering consistent results every time.'). Sample: 300 adult consumers interested in home coffee equipment, recruited via an online panel, balanced for income and self-reported purchase intent.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay a premium price (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the status condition than in the reliability condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the reliability condition than in the status condition.. Decision rule: If the mean purchase intent in the status condition exceeds the mean in the reliability condition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, we conclude that status-driven demand is more likely and recommend developing a status-positioned consumer proposition. If the reliability condition exceeds the status condition by at least 1.5 points, we conclude reliability-driven demand is more likely and recommend a reliability-positioned proposition. If the difference is <1.5 points, we conclude neither mechanism dominates and recommend further research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 consumers recruited from Denmark and the Netherlands, split equally between two groups: one exposed to safety messaging (tap water concerns) and the other exposed to sustainability messaging (environmental preference).. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) for each proposition. 2) WTP: maximum price consumers would pay for each proposition. 3) Messaging preference: which attribute (safety vs sustainability) they would choose.. Predictions: T1: Group exposed to safety messaging will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP for the branded home water filter than the sustainability group.; T2: Group exposed to sustainability messaging will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP for the branded home water filter than the safety group.. Decision rule: If the safety group’s purchase intent is at least 20 percentage points higher than the sustainability group, conclude T1 is more supported. If the sustainability group’s purchase intent is at least 20 percentage points higher, conclude T2. . Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes safety and taste, targeting consumers concerned about tap water quality. Begin with a limited launch in Denmark and the Netherlands to test demand and willingness to pay before broader expansion. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale and maximum price they would pay.. Measure: Purchase intent (7-point scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for each description.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the status-positioned description among high-income participants.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the reliability-positioned description among low-income participants.. Test "Differentiated vs Standard Combi-Steamer Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (self-identified, age 25-55, weekly meal prep). Participants view a product description of a RATIONAL combi-steamer. Condition A receives a premium, easy-to-use, space-saving messaging; Condition B receives a health-focused, steam-cooking messaging. Both descriptions highlight the same core features (steam, easy-c. Sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported cooking frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated reason for purchase.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will achieve higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition A.. Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Condition A and Condition B is at least 1.5 points (e.g., A = 5.5, B = 4.0) and Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 1.5 points, proceed with developing the premium home-cooking. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they value convenience and cost savings over professional services, and a differentiated consumer proposition can capture this demand through premium pricing and direct branding. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking convenient, affordable laundry solutions.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience and lower monthly fees replace the perceived convenience of professional services, prompting adoption.. How value is captured: Electrolux sells a branded consumer product at a premium price, capturing margin through direct sales and brand loyalty.. Assumptions: Homeowners currently rely on professional laundry services or own a laundromat.; They are willing to pay a premium for convenience and cost savings.; Electrolux can effectively brand and distribute a consumer product.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑operated unit, at least 30% of target homeowners will place an order within 12 weeks.; Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the cost of a comparable professional unit..

T2: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they seek resource efficiency and lower long‑term costs, and a differentiated consumer proposition can capture this demand through energy‑efficient features and cost‑saving messaging. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious homeowners and small businesses aiming to reduce utility bills.. Why behaviour changes: Energy‑efficient performance and lower operational costs replace the perceived convenience of professional services, prompting adoption.. How value is captured: Electrolux sells a consumer product with energy‑efficient branding, capturing margin through premium pricing and utility‑cost savings messaging.. Assumptions: Homeowners are aware of and value energy‑efficiency in appliances.; They are willing to pay a premium for reduced utility costs.; Electrolux can effectively communicate energy‑efficiency benefits.. Predictions: In a test offering an energy‑efficient consumer unit, at least 25% of target homeowners will place an order within 12 weeks.; Willingness to pay will be at least 15% above the cost of a comparable professional unit..

Test "Consumer preference test for differentiated home laundry proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two versions of a consumer‑operated laundry unit (one emphasizing convenience and cost savings, the other emphasizing energy efficiency and long‑term cost savings). Participants are recruited from homeowners who have used professional laundry services and are interested in home laundry solutions. Each participant sees one version for 2 minutes and then indicates willingness to pay a premium (20% over the base unit price) and intent to purchase.. Sample: 400 homeowners (200 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and prior experience with professional laundry services.. Measure: Primary measure: share of participants willing to pay the premium price (20% above base unit price). Secondary measure: stated reason for choosing the version (convenience vs. energy efficiency).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will choose the convenience version and express willingness to pay the premium price.; T2: At least 25% of participants will choose the energy‑efficiency version and express willingness to pay the premium price.. Decision rule: If the convenience version achieves at least 30% willingness to pay and the energy‑efficiency version achieves at most 25%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If the energy‑efficiency version achieves at least 25% willingness to pay and the convenience version at most 30%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing energy efficiency. If neither version reaches the respective threshold, do not expand into a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not yet commit to a differentiated consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial-quality home products and that professional customers can reach consumers through retail and wholesale channels. A test is needed to measure willingness to pay for convenience versus energy efficiency. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability and repairability versus performance and price in a recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. It does not address T1's core claim about homeowners' willingness to pay a premium for convenience and cost savings. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not yet commit to a differentiated consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial-quality home products and that professional customers can reach consumers through retail and wholesale channels. A test is needed to measure willingness to pay for convenience versus energy efficiency. Target customer: Homeowners and small businesses seeking convenient, affordable laundry solutions.. Value proposition: A consumer‑operated laundry unit that offers convenience and cost savings (or energy‑efficiency and long‑term cost savings) through a differentiated brand and direct sales channel.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed consumer preference test (400 homeowners, 8 weeks, €18,000) to compare willingness to pay for convenience versus energy‑efficiency versions.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for convenience versus energy efficiency is unknown; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows the energy‑efficiency version achieving at least 25% willingness to pay, the recommendation would shift to emphasize energy efficiency.; If neither version reaches the respective threshold, the recommendation would remain to not expand into a differentiated consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.; Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution that reduces the hassle of bottled water or other alternative water sources. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin offers a membrane that is easy to install, requires minimal maintenance (e.g., cartridge replacement indicator), and integrates with smart home systems, consumers will switch from the hassle of bottled water to a single, self‑s. How value is captured: Lower upfront cost compared to premium membrane, subscription services for maintenance, and data‑driven insights that enhance convenience through smart home integration.. Assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.; A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.; Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher repeat purchase rates than standard membranes.; Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members..

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. T1: Home water purifier owners treat membranes as a durable, low‑maintenance component. If they perceive a membrane as a one‑time purchase, they will not pay a premium for a differentiated consumer proposition, so a manufacturer that offers a differentiated proposition must justify a premium by demonstrating superior durability or longer replacement intervals. Who benefits: Home water purifier owners who value convenience and low ongoing cost.. Why behaviour changes: Owners currently replace membranes every 6‑12 months; a differentiated proposition promising longer replacement intervals or superior performance would shift purchase decisions from frequency to performance.. How value is captured: Value is captured through premium pricing for a differentiated product and through recurring revenue from replacement membranes or service contracts.. Assumptions: Current replacement frequency is 6‑12 months for most membranes.; Performance differences between membrane types are measurable and communicateable to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for longer replacement intervals.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated membrane with a longer replacement claim, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard membrane.; Willingness to pay will be significantly higher for the differentiated proposition compared to a standard one.; Repeat purchase intent will be lower because the perceived cost of replacement is lower..

T2: Home water purifier owners are price‑sensitive and prioritize total cost of ownership (TCO). They will not purchase a differentiated consumer proposition unless the price differential is offset by clear savings on replacement membranes or operational costs, so a manufacturer must demonstrate measurable TCO benefits to justify a premium. Who benefits: Home water purifier owners who are budget‑conscious and value long‑term cost savings.. Why behaviour changes: Owners currently spend on replacement membranes and filter consumables; a differentiated proposition must show that the premium price is balanced by lower replacement frequency or reduced operational costs.. How value is captured: Value is captured through lower total cost of ownership, which can be communicated as a price‑to‑performance trade‑off, allowing the manufacturer to charge a premium while still being competitive.. Assumptions: Replacement membranes currently cost between €20‑€40 per unit.; Operational costs (e.g., electricity, filter consumables) are significant for owners.; Consumers are aware of and can compare TCO across membrane types.. Predictions: In a test comparing a differentiated membrane with a standard one, owners will choose the standard one if the price difference is not justified by savings.; Willingness to pay will be lower for the differentiated proposition when TCO savings are not clearly communicated.; Repeat purchase intent will be higher when the total cost of ownership is presented as lower..

T1 supports, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "The user friendliness continues, as ONE's only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.". Does not show: It does not show that owners perceive membranes as a one-time purchase or that they would not pay a premium for a differentiated proposition..

Test "Membrane Durability vs TCO Choice Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two membrane options (standard vs differentiated) and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent. The differentiated option is described with a longer replacement claim (T1) or a TCO savings claim (T2). Randomization ensures each participant sees only one option.. Sample: 300 adult homeowners with existing water purifiers, recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of the target market.. Measure: WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale). Secondary measure: stated importance of replacement frequency vs TCO savings.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the differentiated option when the claim is about longer replacement intervals.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the differentiated option when the claim is about TCO savings (lower replacement frequency or reduced operational costs).. Decision rule: If the differentiated option's WTP is at least 20% higher than the standard option, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or the TCO claim does not significantly outperform the durability claim, do not invest in a differentiated proposition. If both claims perform equally, conduct further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Aquaporin is in financial distress and has not successfully raised capital, but it also has a consumer product (ONE purifier) and an existing B2B membrane supply agreement with Philips in China. The evidence does not address homeowner willingness to pay a premium for membrane durability, so a differentiated proposition must first be 검증 Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.; Any expansion must consider Simonelli’s existing professional brand and its ability to differentiate without cannibalizing the professional segment.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home barista, small office, travel) with a new product or marketing approach.; 2) Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add consumer-friendly accessories, co‑brands, or a subscription service) without a new differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the professional espresso-equipment business and not pursue consumer propositions.; 4) Partner with or license Simonelli’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Simonelli’s own consumer brand..

T1: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a visible status signal, because conspicuous consumption increases purchase when income is linked to social status. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher margins and brand prestige by selling premium home machines as status items.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers with higher income and status values are more likely to publicly display purchases of visible goods, leading to increased demand when the purchase is framed as a status statement.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price premium home machines and capture higher margins by positioning them as status items rather than purely functional tools.. Assumptions: Status-driven consumers are a significant segment of the home coffee market.; Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to these consumers.; The current professional brand does not cannibalize the consumer proposition.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed as a status item, purchase intent among high-income consumers increases relative to a functional positioning.; Sales of the status-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed purely as a functional product..

T2: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a functional, reliable tool for consistent coffee quality, because reliability reduces purchase hesitation and increases repeat purchases. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains repeat sales and customer loyalty by providing a product that delivers consistent results, increasing overall revenue.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers purchase coffee equipment when they trust the product will perform reliably, reducing the perceived risk of buying a new machine.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price its home machines as reliable, high-quality tools and capture value through repeat purchases and service contracts.. Assumptions: Reliability is a primary purchase driver for home coffee equipment.; Simonelli’s existing professional reputation transfers to consumer positioning.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product they trust to perform consistently.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed on reliability and consistent performance, purchase intent among consumers increases relative to a machine marketed on status.; Sales of the reliability-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed on status..

Test "Status vs Reliability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Participants view two home machine descriptions (Status vs Reliability positioning) and a price point. They indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (WTP).. Sample: 300 adult home coffee consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for income and prior coffee equipment ownership.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average WTP (in euros) for each positioning.. Predictions: T1: Status positioning yields higher purchase intent and higher WTP than reliability positioning.; T2: Reliability positioning yields higher purchase intent and higher WTP than status positioning.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for status positioning is at least 15 percentage points higher than for reliability positioning AND the difference in WTP is at least €50, proceed to develop a status‑focused consumer proposition. If reliability‑positioning intent is at least 15 percentage points higher AND the WTP difference is at least €50, develop a reliability‑focused proposition. If neither difference meets the thresholds, do not expand into consumer propositions.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Simonelli already offers a home-focused machine (Oscar Mood) and a compact home machine (Linea Micra), but it does not prove that status-driven consumers will purchase them. A limited test is needed to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under status versus reliability messaging. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) tests a learning proposition (home-barista lesson) among home espresso enthusiasts, not a status mechanism. It does not address whether status drives purchase decisions, so it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE.

They then indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7‑point scale. The test runs in two parallel groups, each receiving the corresponding product description.. Sample: 200 participants: 100 homeowners (recruited via residential panels) and 100 small‑business decision‑makers (recruited via B2B panels). Randomly assigned to each product group.. Measure: Average WTP and purchase intent (on 7‑point scale).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will report higher WTP and purchase intent for the consumer‑operated unit than for the business unit.; T2: Small‑business decision‑makers will report higher WTP and purchase intent for the business‑operated unit than for the consumer unit.. Who benefits: Home baristas and coffee enthusiasts who enjoy the ritual and quality of espresso.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are increasingly seeking convenience and the social experience of coffee preparation, and they are willing to invest in equipment that meets professional standards.. How value is captured: Simonelli can capture value by offering differentiated consumer products that emphasize ease of use, professional-grade performance, and design, and by selling through retail channels and online platforms.. T2: Consumers are increasingly adopting coffee equipment for personal enjoyment rather than professional use, and they are willing to invest in high-quality, easy-to-use machines for home consumption. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

Predictions: In a survey of health-conscious consumers, at least 30% will state they would purchase a membrane-based home water filter if priced at €200-€300; Purchase intent will be higher in regions with high bottled water consumption and low trust in tap water quality.

Test "Segmented purchase intent survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a health-focused message (perceived water quality risk) or a convenience-focused message (time-saving benefit). Participants are recruited from two segments: health-conscious consumers (n=300) and time-poor consumers (n=300). Both segments see the same product description and price point (proposed €250-€350).. Sample: 300 health-conscious consumers and 300 time-poor consumers, recruited via targeted online panels to match demographic distribution of target markets.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Health-conscious segment will show higher average purchase intent and WTP than time-poor segment, with a difference of at least 1.5 points on the intent scale.; T2: Time-poor segment will show higher average purchase intent and WTP than health-conscious segment, with a difference of at least 1.5 points on the intent scale.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent of the health-conscious segment is at least 1.5 points higher than the time-poor segment, proceed with a differentiated health-focused consumer proposition. If the opposite difference is observed, proceed with. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health-conscious consumers who distrust tap water quality. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, long‑life product that offers superior durability and commercial‑grade performance, and are willing to pay a premium for it. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional Group captures higher margin sales and brand prestige by entering the consumer market with a differentiated offering.. Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Premium Durability vs Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to one of two product concepts and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. Participants view a product description of a self‑service consumer unit (T2) or a differentiated consumer unit (T1) positioned as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance (T1). They are then asked: "How much would you pay a 10% premium over a standard unit for this product?". Sample: 500 adult consumers in the United Kingdom, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income. Stratify by household size to test both concepts.. Measure: Percentage of respondents who state a WTP of at least £100 (or equivalent currency) for the product, and average WTP amount.. Predictions: T1: At least 20% of respondents will state a WTP of at least £100 for the differentiated product, indicating demand for premium durability.; T2: At least 20% of respondents will state a WTP of at least £100 for the self‑service unit, indicating demand for convenience.. Decision rule: If the observed WTP for the differentiated product (T1) is at least 20% and exceeds the WTP for the self‑service unit (T2), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium durability. If the opposite is true, do. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance offering premium durability and reliability. Begin with a limited pilot in retail and wholesale channels to test consumer willingness to pay a premium. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a long‑life, commercial‑grade appliance offering premium durability and reliability. Begin with a limited pilot in retail and wholesale channels to test consumer willingness to pay a premium. Target customer: Residential consumers in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other spaces where self‑service laundry is feasible and demand for commercial‑quality home appliances is growing.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer unit that delivers superior durability, commercial‑grade performance, and a longer warranty, allowing consumers to choose a long‑life appliance over cheaper, disposable alternatives.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (500 UK adults, randomized exposure to premium durability vs convenience concepts, WTP threshold of €100). Use results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.. Uncertainty: The willingness to pay a premium for durability is uncertain; evidence shows consumers are willing to pay extra for long‑life products (T1), but no source directly measures premium price acceptance. Convenience demand (T2) is also uncertain. Would change if: If the test shows the self‑service unit (T2) achieving at least 20% WTP at €100 or higher, indicating stronger convenience demand, we would shift focus to a self‑service consumer unit.; If no test data is available or the results are below the 20% threshold, we would maintain the current professional focus and not pursue consumer expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
