Test "Status vs Reliability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online randomized controlled experiment with two parallel conditions. Participants are shown a description of a home espresso machine (identical product features) and asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale. Condition A receives a status positioning message emphasizing visible status and social signaling. Condition B receives a reliability positioning message emphasizing consistent coffee quality and trust. Participants are randomly assigned to either condition and then asked to indicate willingness to pay a price they would accept.. Sample: 200 adult home coffee consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions.. Measure: Average purchase intent score (on a 7-point scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in Condition A (status positioning) compared to Condition B.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in Condition B (reliability positioning) compared to Condition A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 5.5 vs 4.0), we conclude status positioning drives higher demand and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 1.5 points, we conclude reliability positioning drives higher demand and recommend a reliability-focused proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, we conclude neither positioning is supported and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view one of two product descriptions of a differentiated home water purifier (premium taste/purity vs sustainability/eco-friendly). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to see either the premium messaging or the sustainability messaging.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the premium messaging version.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the sustainability messaging version.. Decision rule: If the premium messaging version achieves a purchase intent score at least 5 points higher than the sustainability messaging version AND the difference in maximum price willingness to pay is at least €20, proceed to develop the premium positioning. If the sustainability messaging version achieves the same or higher score, proceed to develop the sustainability positioning. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, health-focused water purifier, targeting health‑conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for taste and purity. Begin with a limited pilot in Denmark and Turkey to test purchase intent and price sensitivity before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer motivations for a differentiated home water purifier. It tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under a conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, taste, purity, or sustainability. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-AQP-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, health-focused water purifier, targeting health‑conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for taste and purity. Begin with a limited pilot in Denmark and Turkey to test purchase intent and price sensitivity before scaling. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers in Denmark and Turkey who currently use standard water purifiers and are willing to pay a premium for perceived superior taste and purity.. Value proposition: A premium, easy‑to‑use home water purifier that delivers superior taste and purity, with minimal maintenance and a user‑friendly design, justified by a premium price point.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test (500 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and price willingness under premium and sustainability messaging.. Uncertainty: The willingness to pay a premium for taste and purity is uncertain; the test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay more than the current standard‑priced model. Additionally, the sustainability motivation (T2) remains uncertain. Would change if: If the premium messaging version fails to achieve a purchase intent score at least 5 points higher than the sustainability messaging version AND the price difference is less than €20, we would abandon the premium positioning and focus on a; If the sustainability messaging version achieves the same or higher purchase intent score, we would develop a sustainability‑focused proposition instead.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leading them to purchase premium, smart appliances. Who benefits: Home cooks seeking efficient, health-conscious cooking solutions.. Why behaviour changes: If the appliance is marketed as a time-saving, steam‑based cooking system that also offers health benefits (e.g., lower oil use, even cooking), home cooks will be willing to pay a premium over traditional methods.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can capture value by selling a differentiated, branded product at a premium price through direct channels, subscription services, or retail partnerships, leveraging its existing B2B reputation.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay more for convenience and health claims.; Marketing can effectively communicate these benefits to a consumer audience.; The combi-steamer can be adapted to residential use without major redesign.. Predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate intent to purchase a combi-steamer priced 20-30% above a comparable traditional steamer.; Purchase intent will be higher when the product is framed as a health‑enhancing appliance versus a purely convenience appliance.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher household income and exposure to premium kitchen appliances..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they seek a single, versatile appliance that replaces multiple kitchen tools, reducing clutter and saving space, leading them to purchase a premium, integrated system. Who benefits: Home cooks with limited kitchen space and those who prefer a streamlined, multi‑function appliance.. Why behaviour changes: If the appliance can perform multiple cooking functions (steaming, boiling, sautéing) and is marketed as a space‑saving solution, home cooks will be willing to pay more for a compact, integrated unit that simplifies meal preparation.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can capture value by offering a premium‑priced, integrated combi‑steamer through retail channels, subscription services, or partnerships that emphasize space‑efficiency and convenience.. Assumptions: Home cooks prioritize space and convenience over raw cooking performance.; Marketing can effectively communicate the appliance’s versatility and compact design.; The combi‑steamer can be designed to fit standard kitchen layouts without significant modification.. Predictions: Home cooks will rank space‑saving as a top purchase criterion when evaluating a combi‑steamer.; Purchase intent will be higher when the product is positioned as a single‑appliance solution versus a multi‑tool kit.; Sales will be concentrated in urban households with limited kitchen space and higher disposable income..

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition that emphasizes convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology. Begin with a limited pilot in high‑income German households to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Target customer: German households with higher disposable income and exposure to premium kitchen appliances, particularly those seeking efficient, health‑conscious cooking solutions.. Value proposition: A premium, smart combi‑steamer that delivers convenience, health benefits (e.g., lower oil use, even cooking), and modern design, sold through direct channels, subscription services, or retail partnerships.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 6‑week online survey test (400 households) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated combi‑steamer framed on convenience and health.. Uncertainty: The size of the home‑cook market and the exact price premium they are willing to pay remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand from home cooks is lacking; the current B2B focus limits consumer reach.. Would change if: If the survey shows purchase intent below 15% or willingness to pay below €1,200 (20% premium), the recommendation would shift to stay focused on professional kitchens.; If new evidence shows home cooks consistently rank space and versatility as top purchase criteria, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift accordingly.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Predictions: A survey of homeowners will show a higher willingness to purchase a self-service unit compared to a traditional laundromat.; Sales of self-service units will increase in regions where home laundry services are in demand.; Consumer adoption will be driven by convenience and cost savings rather than brand loyalty to established brands..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.. Assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.; A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.; Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.; Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution that reduces the hassle of bottled water or other alternative water sources. Who benefits: Busy households and consumers who currently spend time and money on bottled water, delivery services, or other water alternatives.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin offers a membrane that is easy to install, requires minimal maintenance (e.g., cartridge replacement indicator), and integrates with smart home systems, consumers will switch from the hassle of bottled water to a single, self‑s. How value is captured: Lower upfront cost compared to premium membrane, subscription services for maintenance, and data‑driven insights that enhance convenience through smart home integration.. Assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.; A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.; Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher repeat purchase rates than standard membranes.; Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members..

Does not show: It does not show that a premium positioning would change this preference, nor does it quantify willingness to pay for a differentiated membrane..

Test "Membrane Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Sample: 500 Danish adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a differentiated membrane (premium taste/health vs. low‑maintenance convenience) and self‑reported primary reason for choosing the membrane.. Predictions: T1: Group receiving premium positioning will show WTP at least 20% higher than the low‑maintenance group, and will cite taste or health concerns as primary reason.; T2: Group receiving low‑maintenance positioning will show WTP at least 20% higher than the premium group, and will cite convenience or reduced effort as primary reason.. Decision rule: If premium group WTP ≥ 20% of low‑maintenance group WTP AND taste/health is cited by ≥ 60% of premium group, proceed to develop a differentiated premium proposition. If low‑maintenance WTP ≥ 20% of premium group AND convenience is cited by. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
T1 kept: Simulated warehouse test SYN-D concerns packing errors and does not address consumer perception of premium taste/health benefits, so it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience, particularly in Denmark and potentially other markets where tap water quality is perceived as uncertain.. Value proposition: A differentiated membrane that delivers superior taste, clear health benefits, and easy installation/maintenance, positioned as a premium home purifier that reduces reliance on bottled water.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Membrane Preference Test (500 Danish adults, three groups, willingness to pay and primary reason for choosing). Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a premium positioning pilot.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium‑positioning premium over low‑maintenance convenience is unknown; consumer willingness to pay for taste/health benefits is not quantified; market size for a differentiated unit is uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows low‑maintenance convenience WTP at least 20% higher than premium taste/health WTP, or if a survey reveals convenience as the primary reason for choosing a membrane, we would shift focus to a low‑maintenance proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners and small businesses increasingly adopt self-service laundry solutions as a convenience and cost-saving measure, creating demand for compact, reliable machines that can be installed in limited spaces. Who benefits: Residents, small businesses, and renters who seek convenience and lower laundry costs.. Why behaviour changes: Growing preference for self-service solutions reduces the need for a laundromat or professional provider, and the desire for compact, space-saving equipment makes these machines attractive for home use.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling compact, consumer-focused models through retail and wholesale channels, leveraging its professional-grade reliability and brand reputation to command premium prices.. Assumptions: Homeowners and small businesses are willing to invest in a self-service solution despite higher upfront cost.; The demand for compact machines is driven by space constraints in residential and small commercial settings.; Electrolux can effectively reach these segments through existing retail and wholesale channels.. Predictions: In a test offering a compact consumer model to a sample of homeowners and small businesses, at least 30% will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales conversion rate will be at least 15% of the targeted sample, indicating meaningful demand.; Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a standard professional model..

T2: Commercial property owners and property managers are increasingly seeking energy-efficient, high-performance laundry solutions to reduce operational costs and meet sustainability goals, creating demand for advanced consumer models that can be installed in limited spaces. Who benefits: Commercial property owners, property managers, and tenants who need reliable laundry services while reducing energy consumption.. Why behaviour changes: Growing environmental regulations and cost pressures make energy efficiency a key criterion for new laundry equipment, and the desire to optimize space in small commercial buildings drives demand for compact, efficient machines.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering energy-efficient, high-performance consumer models that meet sustainability standards, and by selling through wholesale channels to property managers and rental companies.. Assumptions: Property owners and managers are willing to invest in energy-efficient equipment despite higher upfront costs.; Sustainability and cost savings are primary drivers for new laundry equipment purchases in commercial settings.; Electrolux can effectively reach these segments through wholesale distribution and property management networks.. Predictions: In a test offering an energy-efficient compact consumer model to a sample of property managers, at least 25% will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales conversion rate will be at least 15% of the targeted sample, indicating meaningful demand.; Willingness to pay will be at least 15% above the price of a standard professional model..

Test "Segmented Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a compact consumer model and an energy-efficient compact model, followed by a purchase intent question.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners and small business owners (targeting T1) and 250 property managers and commercial decision-makers (targeting T2). Recruit via targeted social media and industry forums.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents who state they would purchase the product at a given price point) and willingness to pay (WTP) in a 7-point price range.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners and small business owners exposed to the compact consumer model will have a purchase intent rate of at least 30% and WTP at least 20% above the standard professional model price.; T2: Property managers and commercial decision-makers exposed to the energy-efficient compact model will have a purchase intent rate of at least 25% and WTP at least 15% above the standard professional model price.. Decision rule: If the purchase intent rate for the segment exposed to the compact consumer model is at least 30% and its WTP is at least 20% above the standard professional model price, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for that segment. If the rate is below 25% or the WTP difference is less than 15%, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for that segment.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small businesses with compact, self-service laundry solutions, leveraging Electron’x’s professional-grade reliability and brand reputation to command premium prices through retail and wholesale channels. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small businesses with compact, self-service laundry solutions, leveraging Electron’x’s professional-grade reliability and brand reputation to command premium prices through retail and wholesale channels. Target customer: Homeowners and small business owners who seek convenience, cost savings, and space efficiency for their laundry needs.. Value proposition: Compact, reliable self-service laundry machines that fit limited spaces, offering professional-grade performance and ease of use, enabling consumers to run their own laundry and reduce reliance on laundromats or professional providers.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Segmented Purchase Intent Test (500 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to validate demand for a compact consumer model. If the test meets the decision rule (purchase intent ≥ 30% and willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium), proceed. Uncertainty: The exact size of the residential market and willingness to pay for compact machines are uncertain. Evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality products, but it does not specify whether demand is driven by self-service. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 25% or willingness to pay less than 15% above the standard professional model price, the investment would be reconsidered.; If new evidence shows strong demand for energy-efficient compact machines among property managers, the recommendation would shift toward an energy‑efficient consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water-purifier proposition if they perceive it as a health and safety product, because they trust the membrane technology and are willing to pay a premium for peace of mind. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who want to avoid contaminants and are willing to pay more for a product they believe is safe.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing tap water as unsafe to viewing a membrane purifier as a safe, effective alternative, they will purchase it even if the price is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling it directly to consumers through online channels and retail partners, and leveraging the brand reputation for safety.. Assumptions: Consumers trust membrane technology more than bottled water.; Health concerns are a primary purchase driver for a significant segment of the market.; Price sensitivity is lower for a premium health product than for a standard consumer product.. Predictions: Surveyed health-conscious consumers will indicate higher willingness to pay for a membrane purifier compared to a standard filter.; Sales of the differentiated product will be concentrated among households with children, elderly, or those with known water quality concerns.; Competitor products will not achieve similar premium pricing due to lower perceived safety..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water-purifier proposition if they perceive it as a convenient, low-maintenance solution that fits their lifestyle, because they value ease of use and minimal effort. Who benefits: Time-poor households, busy professionals, and families who prefer products that require little ongoing attention.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purification as a chore to viewing it as a seamless, automatic process, they will choose a product that requires minimal maintenance and installation.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the differentiated product as a plug-and-play solution, offering subscription-based cartridge replacements and direct-to-consumer online sales, and leveraging the brand for convenience.. Assumptions: Maintenance frequency is a significant purchase barrier for consumers.; Convenience and ease of use are more important than price for a segment of the market.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that saves time.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience and low maintenance as top purchase criteria.; Sales of the differentiated product will be higher among households with children, elderly, or those with busy schedules.; Competitor products will not achieve similar adoption rates due to higher perceived effort..

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions if they perceive them as convenient and cost‑effective, leading to higher purchase rates and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional Group gains revenue from consumer sales and can capture value through premium pricing and recurring service contracts.. Why behaviour changes: Growing home‑laundry market and consumer demand for commercial‑quality products create an opportunity for a consumer‑focused offering that addresses homeowner pain points such as space constraints and cost.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell directly to consumers via online channels, retail partnerships, or wholesale to retailers, and capture value through higher margins on consumer units and service revenue.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to purchase commercial‑grade laundry equipment for home use.; Consumer pricing is acceptable compared to professional pricing.; Distribution channels (online, retail) can reach target homeowners effectively.. Predictions: A test offering a consumer‑oriented self‑service unit will achieve at least 5% conversion rate among homeowners who express intent to purchase.; Average transaction value will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional unit.; Repeat purchase rate within 12 months will be at least 15% for customers who initially purchase..

T2: Small businesses and gyms will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions if they need affordable, space‑efficient equipment that reduces labor costs and downtime, leading to higher adoption rates and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional Group gains consumer sales revenue and can capture value through lower unit margins but higher volume and service contracts.. Why behaviour changes: Small businesses and gyms face budget constraints and need equipment that minimizes downtime; consumer‑operated units address these needs by offering compact, low‑cost solutions that can be managed by staff or users.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell directly to consumers via online or retail channels, and capture value through recurring service contracts and volume sales, leveraging its professional expertise to ensure reliability.. Test "Consumer vs Small Business Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners (via residential email list) and 250 small businesses/gyms (via trade association and social media).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy") and WTP (price range in euros).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will have higher purchase intent and WTP than small businesses, with a conversion rate of at least 5% among homeowners and at least 8% among small businesses.; T2: Small businesses will have higher purchase intent and WTP than homeowners, with a conversion rate of at least 8% among small businesses and at least 5% among homeowners.. Decision rule: If homeowners conversion ≥5% and small businesses conversion <8%, recommend consumer proposition for homeowners (T1). If small businesses conversion ≥8% and homeowners conversion <5%, recommend consumer proposition for small businesses (T2). Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.

This directly supports T1, which predicts that highlighting durability and repairability will drive higher conversion among homeowners. New claim: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions if they perceive them as convenient and cost‑effective, leading to higher purchase rates and repeat purchases.. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging the growing residential demand for commercial‑quality home laundry solutions. Begin with a limited pilot offering a compact, self‑service unit priced at a premium but acceptable to consumers, and use online and retail channels to reach the target segment. Target customer: Homeowners in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other residential settings who need reliable, commercial‑grade laundry equipment for home use.. Value proposition: A consumer‑oriented, space‑efficient self‑service unit that delivers professional‑grade washing and drying performance, enabling residents to manage their own laundry with minimal downtime and cost.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Small Business Intent Test (500 respondents, 8‑week survey) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay among homeowners and small businesses. Use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full‑f‑. Uncertainty: The size of the residential market and the price sensitivity of homeowners are uncertain. The test will clarify whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for durability and repairability, which is central to T1.. Would change if: If the test shows homeowners conversion ≥ 5% and small businesses conversion <8%, we would shift focus to a consumer‑focused proposition for small businesses (T2).; If the test shows small businesses conversion ≥ 8% and homeowners conversion <5%, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore other segments.; If new evidence shows that residential demand is much smaller than expected or that small‑business demand is already high, we would abandon the consumer proposition and focus on existing professional segments.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer vs Professional Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two distinct groups. Group A (home barista enthusiasts) receives a product description of a differentiated compact espresso machine (e.g., design-focused, portable) and is asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale). Group B (professional buyers) receives the same description and is asked about intent to purchase a complementary consumer accessory (e.g., compact grinder). Both groups are offered a limited‑time discount code to simulate a purchase decision.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 home barista enthusiasts and 150 professional buyers recruited via social media and industry forums.. Measure: Purchase intent score for Group A (home barista) and Group B (professional) on a 1‑10 scale. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show a purchase intent score of at least 7 (high intent) and a WTP of at least €80, indicating willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated home barista product.; T2: Group B will show a purchase intent score of at least 7 and a WTP of at least €80, indicating willingness to pay a premium for a complementary consumer accessory.. Decision rule: If Group A's purchase intent score is at least 7 and its WTP is at least €80, proceed to develop a differentiated home barista proposition. If Group B's score is at least 7 and its WTP is at least €80, pursue a cross‑selling consumer accessory line. If neither group meets the thresholds, do not invest in a new consumer proposition and maintain the current portfolio.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Convenience vs. Status Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks (self-identified) and professional kitchen users. Each participant views a product description of a RATIONAL combi-steamer and is asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). Messaging is randomized between a convenience framing (time-saving, cleanup reduction) and a status framing (professional‑grade, premium).. Sample: 500 participants: 250 home cooks (self‑identified) and 250 professional kitchen users. Recruit via panel to ensure demographic balance.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average willingness to pay (EUR) for each frame.. Predictions: T1: Home cooks will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the convenience frame than for the status frame.; T2: Home cooks will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the status frame than for the convenience frame.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay for the convenience frame exceeds the status frame by ≥ €50, recommend developing a differentiated home‑cook proposition focused on convenience. If the status frame exceeds the convenience frame by ≥ €50, recommend a premium, status‑focused offering. If neither difference meets the thresholds, recommend no expansion (maintain current B2B focus).. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed convenience‑vs‑status messaging test (or a smaller pilot) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent for the convenience framing. Would change if: If the test shows the status framing generates significantly higher willingness to pay than the convenience framing, we would reconsider a premium, status‑focused offering.; If the test fails to show a meaningful difference between the two frames, we would recommend no expansion and maintain the current B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

T1: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer because they value convenience, health benefits (steaming), and premium performance, leading them to pay a premium price for a consumer-friendly version. Who benefits: Home cooks seeking efficient, healthy cooking solutions. Why behaviour changes: They shift from traditional cooking methods to a single appliance that combines steaming, boiling, and baking, reducing kitchen clutter and preparation time.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can sell a consumer-branded combi-steamer at a premium price through retail channels, capturing higher margins than its current commercial sales.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay more for a branded, consumer-oriented version of a commercial product; The combi-steamer's health benefits (steaming) are perceived as a unique selling point; Distribution channels exist for consumer appliances. Predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate intent to purchase a consumer-branded combi-steamer at a price 20-30% above the commercial price; Sales of a consumer-branded version will exceed sales of a generic combi-steamer in the same market segment.

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer because they seek a single, versatile appliance that replaces multiple kitchen tools, reducing purchase and maintenance costs, and they trust RATIONAL's reputation for commercial excellence. Who benefits: Home cooks with limited kitchen space and budget who want a single, high-performance appliance. Why behaviour changes: They shift from owning multiple separate appliances to a single, integrated system that handles steaming, boiling, and baking, simplifying meal preparation.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can sell a consumer-branded combi-steamer at a premium price, leveraging its existing brand equity and distribution network to capture higher margins.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay more for a single, integrated appliance; RATIONAL's commercial reputation transfers to consumer perception; Consumer distribution channels are available for a premium appliance. Predictions: Home cooks will indicate intent to purchase a single-combi-steamer at a price 20-30% above a comparable multi-appliance setup; Sales of a consumer-branded combi-steamer will be higher in households with limited kitchen space than in households with ample space.

T1: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they seek convenience, health benefits, and premium performance, willing to pay a premium for a compact, smart, or subscription-based system that simplifies cooking. Who benefits: Home cooks gain time-saving, healthier cooking; RATIONAL benefits from higher-margin sales and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: Growing demand for time-efficient appliances and health-conscious consumers prefer steam cooking over traditional methods; a differentiated proposition signals innovation and aligns with modern lifestyle values.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for smart features, subscription services, and direct-to-consumer sales capture higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Assumptions: Home cooks have discretionary income to invest in premium kitchen appliances.; Smart or subscription models can be marketed effectively to individual buyers.; Regulatory and safety standards allow residential use of commercial technology.. Predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a combi-steamer with smart features compared to a standard model.; Pilot sales of a subscription-based service will generate at least 10% monthly recurring revenue within 12 weeks.; Social media engagement with a differentiated proposition will exceed baseline by at least 30% compared to a generic product launch..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value professional-quality cooking performance and are willing to pay for a device that replicates commercial kitchen standards, even if it is larger and more expensive than existing residential models. Who benefits: Home cooks gain access to high-end cooking capabilities; RATIONAL benefits from premium pricing and brand extension as a leader in professional cooking technology.. Why behaviour changes: Growing interest in gourmet home cooking and desire for equipment that matches professional standards drive demand for devices that deliver consistent, high-quality results, even if they are larger and more complex.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for advanced features, limited edition designs, and direct-to-consumer sales capture higher margins than bulk B2B sales, leveraging RATIONAL’s reputation as a technology leader.. Test "Home Cooks Willingness-to-Pay Survey Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging to home cooks (self-identified) recruited via social media and kitchen forums. Participants view a product description of a differentiated combi-steamer (either a compact smart model or a professional‑grade model) and are asked: “How much would you pay for this product?”. Sample: 400 home cooks (200 per arm) recruited in Germany and Austria, balanced for age, gender, and kitchen ownership. Recruitment cost €1,000.. Measure: Percentage of participants who indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for the smart‑grade model and at least 30% more for the professional‑grade model.. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of respondents will choose the smart‑grade model and indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more.; T2: At least 60% of respondents will choose the professional‑grade model and indicate willingness to pay at least 30% more.. Decision rule: If the smart‑grade model achieves ≥ 60% willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium and the professional‑grade model achieves ≥ 60% willingness to pay ≥ 30% premium, proceed with a differentiated home‑cook proposition targeting both segments. If only. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer) targeting individual buyers, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology and brand reputation. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer) targeting individual buyers, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology and brand reputation. Target customer: Home cooks in Germany and Austria who value convenience, health benefits, and premium performance, and are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated combi‑steamer.. Value proposition: A compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer that simplifies cooking, offers health‑conscious steam cooking, and aligns with modern lifestyle values, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 12‑week, €20,000 willingness‑to‑pay survey pilot to validate demand for a differentiated smart‑grade model and its willingness‑to‑pay premium.. Uncertainty: The size of the home‑cook market and the exact willingness‑to‑pay premium remain uncertain; the pilot will resolve this.. Would change if: If the pilot shows <60% willingness to pay ≥ 20% premium for the smart‑grade model, or if a separate test shows strong demand for a professional‑grade model with ≥ 30% premium, the recommendation would shift toward a professional‑grade home; If new evidence shows home cooks overwhelmingly prefer traditional cooking methods or are unwilling to pay a premium for combi‑steamers, the recommendation would shift toward staying focused on professional kitchens.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a visible status signal, because conspicuous consumption increases purchase when income is linked to social status. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher margins and brand prestige by selling premium home machines as status items.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers with higher income and status values are more likely to publicly display purchases of visible goods, leading to increased demand when the purchase is framed as a status statement.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price premium home machines and capture higher margins by positioning them as status items rather than purely functional tools.. Assumptions: Status-driven consumers are a significant segment of the home coffee market.; Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to these consumers.; The current professional brand does not cannibalize the consumer proposition.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed as a status item, purchase intent among high-income consumers increases relative to a functional positioning.; Sales of the status-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed purely as a functional product..

T2: Home coffee consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a functional, reliable tool for consistent coffee quality, because reliability reduces purchase hesitation and increases repeat purchases. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains repeat sales and customer loyalty by providing a product that delivers consistent results, increasing overall revenue.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers purchase coffee equipment when they trust the product will perform reliably, reducing the perceived risk of buying a new machine.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price its home machines as reliable, high-quality tools and capture value through repeat purchases and service contracts.. Assumptions: Reliability is a primary purchase driver for home coffee equipment.; Simonelli’s existing professional reputation transfers to consumer positioning.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product they trust to perform consistently.. Predictions: When a home machine is marketed on reliability and consistent performance, purchase intent among consumers increases relative to a machine marketed on status.; Sales of the reliability-positioned home machine will be higher than sales of a similar machine marketed on status..

Test "Subscription vs Premium Positioning Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 German adults (250 per arm) recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: 1) WTP: maximum monthly fee (EUR) a respondent would pay for the device. 2) Choice: percentage selecting "Subscription" vs "Premium" option. 3) Intent to purchase: binary (would buy).. Predictions: T1: Subscription arm shows higher WTP and higher "Subscription" choice than Premium arm; Premium arm shows low intent.; T2: Premium arm shows higher WTP and higher "Premium" choice than Subscription arm; Subscription arm shows low intent.. Decision rule: If Subscription arm WTP ≥ €30 and Premium arm WTP < €20, recommend Subscription positioning (T1). Else if Premium arm WTP ≥ €30 and Subscription arm WTP < €20, recommend Premium positioning (T2). If neither condition is met, inconclusive and no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B relationships and subscription model to capture recurring revenue. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B relationships and subscription model to capture recurring revenue. Target customer: Home cooks who value convenience, time-saving solutions, and recurring revenue, particularly younger, tech-savvy consumers.. Value proposition: A subscription-based combi-steamer that reduces upfront cost and provides ongoing updates, while RATIONAL captures value through recurring subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Subscription vs Premium Positioning Test (500 German adults, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent for subscription versus premium positioning.. Uncertainty: The size of the home cook market and their willingness to pay for a subscription model are unknown. The test will resolve whether subscription demand is sufficient to justify expansion.. Would change if: If the test shows subscription WTP < €20 and premium WTP ≥ €30, we would shift to premium positioning (T2).; If the test shows no significant difference between subscription and premium arms, we would recommend no expansion and stay focused on professional kitchens.; If new evidence shows strong home cook demand for professional-grade status, we would reconsider premium positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Premium vs. Budget Combi-Steamer Choice Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to either a premium-priced combi-steamer (high-end design, health benefits, premium price) or a budget-priced combi-steamer (durable, commercial-grade, lower price). They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each scenario.. Predictions: T1: Participants assigned to the premium-priced scenario will report higher purchase intent and be willing to pay at least 20% more than the budget scenario.; T2: Participants assigned to the budget-priced scenario will report higher purchase intent and be willing to pay at least 20% less than the premium scenario.. Decision rule: If the premium scenario's average purchase intent exceeds the budget scenario's by at least 15 points (e.g., premium intent = 7.5 vs. budget intent = 5.5), proceed to develop a differentiated home-cook proposition. If the premium scenario's average price willingness to pay is at least 20% higher than the budget scenario's, justify premium pricing. If neither condition is met, maintain focus on professional kitchens.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on RATIONAL’s combi-steamer technology, leveraging its premium positioning and health benefits to capture discretionary home-cook demand. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to either a homeowner group (n=200) or a small business/housing provider group (n=200). Each group sees a product description of a consumer‑operated machine (e.g., compact washing/drying unit) and a professional‑grade machine. Homeowners are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. Small‑business/housing providers are asked to indicate purchase intent and whether they would purchase at a given price point. The test also includes a follow‑up survey to measure repeat service usage.. Sample: 200 homeowners and 200 small businesses/housing providers, recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each group and average price willingness to pay. Secondary measure: repeat service usage (binary: ≥ 3 cycles per year).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a premium for the consumer‑operated machine than small‑business/housing providers.; T2: Small‑business/housing providers will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a premium for the consumer‑operated machine than homeowners.. Decision rule: If homeowners’ purchase intent ≥ 7 and their average price willingness to pay ≥ €400, and small‑business/housing providers’ purchase intent ≤ 5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If small‑business/housing providers’ purchase intent ≥ 7 and their average price willingness to pay ≥ €400, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition targeting small businesses. If neither threshold is met, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑conscious product that signals quality and convenience, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking high‑performance water purification and premium branding.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view the product as a status or health symbol rather than a functional necessity, they will be willing to purchase it at a higher price.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the product as a premium consumer item, selling through retail channels, and leveraging its brand to command higher margins.. Assumptions: Consumers associate premium branding with superior performance.; There is a segment of consumers willing to pay a premium for a differentiated water purifier.; Retail distribution can reach this segment effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent will be higher among health‑conscious consumers compared to a standard‑priced product.; Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a premium‑branded purifier than for a generic one..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it offers a service or subscription model that reduces ongoing maintenance and provides performance monitoring, leading them to choose a subscription over a one‑time purchase. Who benefits: Consumers who find maintenance cumbersome and value convenience and ongoing support.. Why behaviour changes: If maintenance becomes a barrier, consumers will switch to a subscription that automates replacement and monitoring, reducing perceived effort and cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture recurring revenue through subscription fees, leveraging its membrane technology to provide continuous service and data insights.. Assumptions: Maintenance is a significant pain point for current purifier owners.; Consumers are willing to pay a recurring fee for convenience.; The subscription model can be integrated without disrupting existing product use.. Predictions: In a test offering a subscription‑based maintenance package, churn rate will be lower than for a one‑time purchase.; Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay a monthly fee of €10‑€15 for maintenance and monitoring services..

Test "Premium vs Subscription Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a premium‑priced differentiated purifier with a one‑time purchase option and is asked about willingness to pay a premium. Group B sees the same product but offers a subscription‑based maintenance package with recurring monthly fees and is asked about willingness to subscribe. Both groups are asked about reasons for choosing each option.. Sample: 400 adult consumers interested in water purification, recruited via an online panel. 200 per group to ensure balanced representation.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for the premium option (Group A) and willingness to subscribe (Group B). Secondary measure: stated reasons for choosing each option.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher WTP for the premium option than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher willingness to subscribe than Group A.. Decision rule: If the difference in WTP between the premium option and subscription option is at least €15, proceed with a differentiated premium proposition. If the subscription option's WTP is at least €15 higher than the premium option, proceed with a subscription model. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Public evidence shows Aquaporin already sells membranes to consumer brands (e.g., Philips in China, Vestel in Turkey) and has a consumer brand (ONE). The only public evidence supporting a differentiated consumer proposition is the premium-priced ONE purifier, which does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium price. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct a small-scale pilot test (e.g., a premium-priced differentiated purifier offered to a niche segment) to validate willingness to pay before scaling.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium segment and actual willingness to pay remain uncertain; public evidence does not confirm demand for a differentiated proposition.. Would change if: If a pilot shows purchase intent above 20% and willingness to pay at least 20% more than a standard-priced product, proceed with a differentiated premium proposition.; If a pilot shows strong subscription uptake (e.g., >30% willingness to subscribe) and recurring revenue potential, reconsider a subscription model.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners and renters increasingly view laundry as a convenience service, leading to demand for self‑service options that reduce wait times and improve convenience. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who lack on‑site laundry facilities and prefer quick, self‑serviced cleaning.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience and time‑saving become primary purchase drivers; self‑service removes the need to schedule a machine or wait for a person to clean.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering compact, self‑service machines sold directly to consumers through retail or online channels, leveraging its professional‑grade reliability to command premium pricing.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for self‑service convenience over traditional laundromats.; Regulatory and safety standards for consumer‑grade machines are met without compromising professional performance.; Retail distribution channels can effectively reach and serve individual buyers.. Predictions: In a test market, self‑service machines will achieve higher adoption rates among renters and homeowners compared to traditional laundromats.; Surveyed consumers will report convenience as the top reason for choosing a self‑service machine.; Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional model..

T2: Small businesses and hospitality operators increasingly adopt self‑service laundry to reduce labor costs and improve operational efficiency, creating demand for compact, reliable machines that fit limited spaces. Who benefits: Small hotels, gyms, marina staff, and other small‑business operators with limited space and high turnover of laundry tasks.. Why behaviour changes: Cost savings and efficiency gains outweigh the upfront investment; self‑service eliminates the need for staff to monitor and maintain machines.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering compact, professional‑grade machines sold through wholesale channels to small‑business customers, leveraging its reputation for reliability and serviceability.. Assumptions: Small businesses are willing to invest in self‑service laundry to reduce labor costs.; The machines meet the performance and durability standards expected by these customers.; Wholesale distribution can effectively reach and serve small‑business operators.. Predictions: In a test market, small‑business customers will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay compared to homeowners.; Surveyed small‑business owners will cite cost savings and space efficiency as primary reasons for choosing a self‑service machine.; Adoption rates among small‑business operators will be at least 15% higher than among homeowners..

Test "Segmented Messaging Test for Self-Service Laundry" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three message conditions: (1) Homeowner convenience (self-service convenience, time savings, and premium pricing); (2) Small business efficiency (labor cost savings, space efficiency, and compact design); (3) Control (neutral message). After viewing the assigned message, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 adults (250 homeowners/renters and 250 small‑business owners) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than small‑business owners, and both segments will be driven primarily by convenience messaging.; T2: Small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than homeowners, and both segments will be driven primarily by efficiency messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for homeowners is at least 10 points higher than for small‑business owners, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed with a differentiated homeowner proposition. If the difference is less than 10 points or not statistically significant, proceed with a small‑business proposition. If both segments show similar intent differences, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters, emphasizing self-service convenience and premium pricing. Begin with a limited retail pilot to test demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Begin with a limited retail pilot to test demand before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and renters who lack on-site laundry facilities and seek quick, self‑serviced cleaning.. Value proposition: Compact, professional‑grade self‑service machines that deliver commercial‑grade performance at a premium price, addressing the growing residential demand for convenience and quality.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed segmented messaging test (500 participants, 3 conditions) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for homeowners versus small‑business owners. Use the decision rule: if homeowners show at least 10 points higher. Uncertainty: The size of the residential market and willingness to pay for premium self‑service machines are unknown. Small‑business demand is also uncertain; the test will clarify whether small‑business owners are willing to invest in self‑service.. Would change if: If the test shows small‑business owners exceeding homeowners in purchase intent and willingness to pay, we would shift focus to a small‑business proposition.; If residential demand proves weak or no premium pricing is observed, we would reconsider expansion or explore alternative routes to market.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Design vs. Time-Saving Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Both conditions include a detailed product description of a RATIONAL combi-steamer. Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 home cooks (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure representation across age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Predictions: T1: Design Condition will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Time-Saving Condition.; T2: Time-Saving Condition will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Design Condition.. Who benefits: The management team and existing shareholders who prioritize stability and growth in their core business.. Why behaviour changes: The company may choose to avoid the complexities and uncertainties of entering a new consumer market, such as water purifiers, to focus on its established expertise and customer base.. How value is captured: By maintaining its core business, Aquaporin A/S can continue to generate stable revenue and market share, avoiding the potential risks and costs associated with a new product line.. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.. Assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.; A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.; Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.; Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution that reduces the hassle of bottled water or other alternative water sources. Who benefits: Busy households and consumers who currently spend time and money on bottled water, delivery services, or other water alternatives.. Why behaviour changes: If Aquaporin offers a membrane that is easy to install, requires minimal maintenance (e.g., cartridge replacement indicator), and integrates with smart home systems, consumers will switch from the hassle of bottled water to a single, self‑s. How value is captured: Lower upfront cost compared to premium membrane, subscription services for maintenance, and data‑driven insights that enhance convenience through smart home integration.. Assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.; A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.; Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.; Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher repeat purchase rates than standard membranes.; Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members..

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water filter if they perceive it as a health benefit and trust the brand, because they are willing to pay a premium for perceived safety and taste.
